passage: Saturday, 9 pm. First class done. Twenty students from classes eight to ten in the school near my aunt's village crammed into one room with six borrowed laptops. Neelam, the science teacher who let me use the room, sat at the back. I'd planned an hour on variables; it took forty minutes because half the group couldn't type yet, so we switched to drawing flowcharts on paper and typing in pairs. Learned already: pairs work, short tasks work, my slides don't. The power went out twice, and the kids clapped in the dark when it came back. I'm not planning anything big yet. Four more Saturdays, then I'll write down what worked and only then decide what next. Tired feet, full head. — Farida

qa.q: How does Farida feel at the end of the day?
qa.a: Farida feels tired but energised, with tired feet and a full head from what was learned.

qa.q: What other approach could Farida use before the next class?
qa.a: Farida could ask Neelam and a few students what they want to learn, since it shows what is worth teaching before more slides are made.

qa.q: How might Neelam see the class?
qa.a: Neelam probably sees a useful start, since twenty students turned up and stayed engaged even when the power went out.

grounding: Shows a software worker starting with free Saturday coding classes for twenty village school students and learning what works before planning anything larger.

Sachin: how did the first class go?
Karthik: 20 kids, 6 laptops, 1 projector that died at 11 😅
Sachin: so a disaster
Karthik: no! they loved it. we did the drawing-with-code thing on paper when the projector died
Sachin: what did you learn
Karthik: 1. they need more time per laptop, so pairs not groups of 4. 2. the headmaster wants something the teachers can continue on weekdays. 3. hindi instructions work better than english
Sachin: you still planning that app for 100 schools?
Karthik: not yet. first I want 3 months of Saturdays here. see what sticks. then think bigger
Sachin: can I come next Saturday? I have 2 old laptops
Karthik: yes!! that's 8 laptops 🙏

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
subtype: Approach: starting with a small pilot [Action]
passage:
Every Sunday morning, Ramesh took the 7 a.m. bus from Kolhapur to his native village and walked to the zilla parishad school. Omkar Sir, the maths teacher, unlocked the one room with computers: four old desktops and a borrowed laptop. Twenty children from Classes 6 to 8 were already waiting on the steps.
Ramesh didn't have a big plan. He had a notebook where he wrote, after each class, what worked and what didn't. Week 2: children share better in pairs than in fours. Week 4: games work, lectures don't. Week 6: power cut, so paper puzzles. Week 9: two girls built a simple quiz without help.
Omkar Sir started staying for the whole class. 'If this keeps going,' he said in week ten, 'I could run a Wednesday session myself.' Ramesh wrote that down too.

qa.a: Two girls built a simple quiz without help.

qa.q: What does Omkar Sir staying for the whole class suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Omkar Sir became interested and hopeful, enough to consider running a session himself.

qa.q: Why is Ramesh's notebook a good part of the pilot?
qa.a: It records what works, like pairs and games, so any bigger plan is built on real lessons.

qa.q: How might the children experience the Sunday classes?
qa.a: They get hands-on games and puzzles, and some, like the two girls, gain confidence building things themselves.

grounding: It shows someone teaching free weekend coding classes to twenty students in a village school and learning what works before planning anything larger.
